items.followUp: How does an enzyme’s active site interact with its substrate?

rubric.why: The substrate binds at the enzyme’s active site.
rubric.description: States that the active site binds or fits the substrate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate binds or fits at the active site.

rubric.why: The active site enables the enzyme to catalyse the reaction and form product.
rubric.description: Describes the active site’s role in catalysis or product formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the active site helps catalyse the reaction or convert the substrate into product.

modelAnswer: The active site is the specific region of an enzyme to which its substrate binds.
It enables the enzyme to catalyse the reaction and convert the substrate into product.

items.followUp: Who introduced the term protoplasm, and in what year?

rubric.why: Wilhelm Kühne used the term enzyme.
rubric.description: Names Kühne as the person who used the term enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving Kühne’s surname.

rubric.why: The term enzyme was used in 1878.
rubric.description: Gives the year the term was used.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct year.

modelAnswer: Wilhelm Kühne used the term enzyme in 1878.

items.followUp: What is the approximate length of the human small intestine?

rubric.why: The human oesophagus is about 25 centimetres long.
rubric.description: Gives the approximate length of the human oesophagus.

rubric.why: The length is expressed in centimetres.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating centimetres or cm.

modelAnswer: The human oesophagus is about 25 centimetres (cm) long.

items.followUp: Differentiate between saturated and unsaturated fatty acids by their bonds.

rubric.why: Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds.
rubric.description: States the bond feature of saturated fatty acids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that saturated fatty acids have no double bonds or only single bonds.

accept: one or more carbon carbon double bonds
rubric.why: Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more carbon–carbon double bonds.
rubric.description: States the bond feature of unsaturated fatty acids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds.

modelAnswer: Saturated fatty acids have no carbon–carbon double bonds.
Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more carbon–carbon double bonds.

items.followUp: Name the three types of plastids and state one function of each.

rubric.why: Plastids are organelles found in plant cells.
rubric.description: Identifies plastids as organelles found in plant cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing plastids as organelles of plant cells.

rubric.why: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Chromoplasts contain pigments that give colour to flowers and fruits.
rubric.description: Links chromoplasts with pigments or colour.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chromoplasts contain pigments or give colour.

rubric.why: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food.
rubric.description: States the food-storage role of leucoplasts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that leucoplasts store food.

rubric.why: Leucoplasts may store starch, oils or proteins.
rubric.description: Names a food material stored by leucoplasts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming starch, oils or proteins as a stored material.

modelAnswer: Plastids are organelles found in plant cells.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
Chromoplasts contain pigments that give colour to flowers and fruits.
Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food.
Leucoplasts may store starch, oils or proteins.

items.followUp: State the rules for writing the scientific name of an organism using binomial nomenclature.

rubric.why: A scientific name in binomial nomenclature consists of two words.
rubric.description: States that a scientific name has two parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the name consists of two words or names.

rubric.why: The first word is the genus name and begins with a capital letter.
rubric.description: Identifies the first word as the capitalised genus name.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the first word as the genus and stating that it begins with a capital letter.

rubric.why: The second word is the species name and begins with a small letter.
rubric.description: Identifies the second word as the species name, beginning with a small letter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the second word as the species name and stating that it begins with a small letter.

rubric.why: Scientific names are written in italics, or underlined separately when handwritten.
rubric.description: Gives the convention for writing scientific names.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that scientific names are italicised or underlined when handwritten.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of naming organisms with two words.
The first word is the genus name and begins with a capital letter.
The second word is the species name and begins with a small letter.
The two words are written in italics, or underlined separately when handwritten; for example, Homo sapiens.
